# How to Check if a Suspicious Message Is a Scam, and What an AI Assistant Can and Can't Do

> **In short:** Don't click, reply or call the number in a suspicious message. Check it with the company or person using contact details you already know are real, then report it and delete it. An AI assistant can explain a message's warning signs as an optional extra, but it can be wrong and it can't tell you who really sent the message, so keep your personal details out of the chat.

Scam messages can look convincing: a familiar company name, a worried tone, a link that seems to fix everything. The FTC's advice is simple. If you have no account with the company, or don't know the person who wrote, review the warning signs, report the message and delete it. If you do, contact them using a phone number or website you know is real. This guide follows that advice in six steps and shows where an AI assistant can help as a second opinion. One warning up front: an assistant only sees the text you give it and can be wrong, so the real check always happens outside the chat.

## Before you start
- The suspicious message, left as it is so you can report it. Don't tap anything in it.
- A phone number or website you already know is real, for the company or person it claims to be from.
- Optional: an AI assistant, for Step 3 only. Never paste passwords, one-time codes, or full card, bank account or ID numbers into any chat.

## Step 1 — Stop: don't click, reply or call the number in the message
Links and attachments in a suspicious message can install harmful software, and its contact details can lead to the scammer, not the company. So don't click a link or open an attachment, don't reply (or use an "unsubscribe" link), and don't call a number the message gives you. Honest organizations give you time to decide, so a message that pushes you to act right now is already showing a warning sign.
💬 Example: a text says "Your account is locked. Confirm your details at example.com/verify within 24 hours." Leave the link alone and keep reading.
You'll know it worked when you haven't tapped, replied or called anything, and the message is still there, unchanged.

## Step 2 — Look for the warning signs
The FTC lists four signs of a scam: the sender pretends to be from an organization you know, says there's a problem or a prize, pressures you to act immediately, and tells you to pay in a specific way, such as cryptocurrency, a wire transfer, a payment app or gift cards, or by depositing a check and sending money back. For phishing, also watch for a generic greeting, requests to confirm personal or financial information, or a link to update your payment details. CISA adds urgent or emotional language, shortened links you can't trust, and addresses or links with small mistakes in them. Don't count on spelling mistakes: in the era of AI, CISA notes, some emails now have perfect grammar and spelling.

Then ask yourself: "Do I have an account with this company, or do I know this person?" If not, treat the message as suspicious, because it could be a scam, and skip ahead to Step 5.
💬 Example: "Billing problem on your account. Update your payment details now using this link." It claims a problem, creates pressure and asks for payment details: three warning signs in one short message.
You'll know it worked when you can name the warning signs the message shows, or you've noticed it doesn't match any account or person you know.

## Step 3 — Optional: ask an AI assistant to explain the message
An AI assistant can walk you through a message's warning signs in plain language, but treat it as an optional extra, because the official advice doesn't depend on it. Keep four limits in mind:
- It only sees the text you paste in, so it can't confirm who sent the message or whether a link is safe.
- It can be wrong in either direction. The makers of these assistants say themselves that answers can be mistaken and should be checked against reliable sources.
- A "this looks fine" answer is never permission to click. Step 4 still applies.
- A chat isn't a private notebook: services can keep conversations, and some use them to improve their models or let people review them.

Before you paste, remove your name, address, phone number, account, card and ID numbers, passwords and verification codes, and anyone else's personal details. If the message is full of them, describe it in your own words instead, or skip this step.
💬 Example prompt: "Here is a message I received, with personal details removed: [paste here]. Without clicking anything, explain which warning signs of phishing or a scam it shows, if any, and remind me how to check it safely."
You'll know it worked when the answer points to parts of the message you can see yourself, and you haven't put anything into the chat that you wouldn't want stored.

## Step 4 — Check with the real company or person
This step decides it. If the message claims to be from a company, contact that company using a phone number or website you know is real, such as the number on the back of your card, never the contact details in the message. If it claims to be from a person you know, reach them through a number or chat you already use, not by replying. If they say they didn't send it, treat it as a scam and go to Step 5. If it was genuine but unexpected, still don't use its links: go to the company's site or app yourself. If you can't confirm it, treat it as suspicious. Talking it over with someone you trust can also help.
You'll know it worked when the company or person has confirmed the message, or told you it isn't theirs, through a channel you chose yourself.

## Step 5 — Report it, then delete it
The FTC suggests: forward a phishing email to reportphishing@apwg.org; forward a phishing text to 7726 (SPAM); use the report option in your email or messaging app; and report it to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov. You can also file a report with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov. Outside the US, contact your local police or consumer protection agency. Once you've reported it, delete the message.
You'll know it worked when the message is reported and gone from your inbox.

## Step 6 — If you already clicked, replied or paid
Don't panic: there are clear next steps. If you gave out a Social Security, credit card or bank account number, go to IdentityTheft.gov for steps based on what you shared. If you gave out a password, create a new strong one, change it anywhere else you used it, and turn on two-factor authentication. If you think you clicked a link or opened an attachment that downloaded harmful software, or you gave someone access to your device, update your security software, run a scan and remove anything it flags.

If you paid, contact the company you paid with right away, using the number on the back of your card or on the gift card: your bank or credit union, card issuer, payment app, wire transfer company, gift card issuer, or the cryptocurrency exchange or ATM operator. Tell them it was a scam and ask for the payment to be reversed. Getting money back isn't guaranteed, and it's often hard with cryptocurrency. Then report the message as in Step 5.
You'll know it worked when you've contacted the right company or service and reported what happened.

## Common mistakes
- **Treating the AI's answer as the final word.** An assistant can miss a scam or flag a genuine message by mistake. Fix: use it only to point at things you can check yourself, then do Step 4.
- **Pasting personal details into the chat, or replying, calling or tapping "just to check".** The first shares what you shouldn't; the second can put you in touch with the scammer. Fix: Steps 1, 3 and 4.
- **Relying on spelling mistakes.** Fix: judge the message by what it asks you to do (Step 2).

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** when a text or email claims a problem with your account or a delivery and asks for details or payment, pause, check with the real company, report it and delete it.
- **For your business or work:** if a message asks you to change payment details or send money, confirm it using contact details you already have, and follow your workplace's rules for reporting.
- **If you're just getting started:** Steps 1 and 4 protect you most. Also turn on multi-factor authentication for your important accounts: the FTC says it makes it harder for scammers to log in even if they have your password.

## Try it now
Find one message you've been unsure about, or an old junk email. Without tapping anything, go through Step 2, then check it with the real company (Step 4), report it and delete it.
